title: General Quantification of Covariate and Concept Shifts
claim: Standard entropic OT estimators badly overestimate distance as dimension grows and barely improve with more samples; our debiased estimator stays accurate.
layout: 3 line-plot panels in a row, shared legend style, ours in orange
description: Three side-by-side line plots, each with an 'Empirical Distance' y-axis and a subpanel caption below. (a) plots distance against dimension d from 0 to 100. Two blue curves, the traditional estimator at N=1000 and N=50000, climb steeply to about 11–12. Two orange curves, the debiased estimator labeled '(ours)', stay flat near zero. (b) plots distance against N^(-1/d) for d=50, 70 and 90, shown as blue and teal lines. Dashed diagonals and pink arrows mark where N=100 and N=50000 fall. (c) plots distance against true Wasserstein-1 distance from 0 to 25. The blue curves start at a high offset of about 9 and bend toward the diagonal. The orange debiased curves lie exactly on the dashed diagonal. The eye goes first to the gap between blue and orange in (a).
caption: (a)–(c) show the empirical distance from entropic optimal transport $(\beta = 0.001)$ versus dimension $d$, sample size $N$, and true Wasserstein-1 distance. In (a)–(b), $\hat\eta$ and $\hat\eta'$ are independent empirical measures from high-dimensional standard normals, thus the true distance is zero. The traditional estimator $W_\beta(\hat\eta,\hat\eta')$ greatly overestimates as $d$ increases, as shown in (a), and even a much larger $N$ only brings a small improvement, as shown in (b). In (c), with $d = 70$, $\hat\eta_t$ is the empirical measure of shifted standard normal $\mathcal{N}(t,I)$, whose true Wasserstein-1 distance to the standard normal is $\|t\|$. Our debiased estimator remains accurate in every case.
abstract: Generalization under distribution shift remains a core challenge in modern machine learning, yet existing learning bound theory is limited to narrow, idealized settings and is non-estimable from samples. In this paper, we bridge the gap between theory and practical applications. We first show that existing definition of concept shift breaks when the source and target supports mismatch. Leveraging entropic optimal transport, we propose a key notion: $Î³^{*}\!$-concept shifts, and derive a general error bound unifying covariate and $Î³^{*}\!$-concept shifts, which applies to broad loss functions, label spaces, and stochastic labeling. We further develop estimators for these shifts with concentration guarantees, and the DataShifts algorithm, which can quantify distribution shifts and estimate the error bound in most applications - a rigorous and general tool for analyzing learning error under distribution shift.
